stem: A wire is placed just above a magnetic compass and a switch is closed so that current flows through the wire. What happens to the compass needle?
options: It stays exactly where it was before
It turns away from its original direction
It starts spinning round without stopping
It loses its magnetism permanently
explanation: Correct option: (B). A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, which acts on the tiny magnet in the compass and deflects it from its original direction. The needle does not stay still, does not spin continuously, and does not lose its magnetism; it returns to its original direction when the current stops.

stem: Which scientist discovered in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic field?
options: Alessandro Volta
Luigi Galvani
H. C. Oersted
Michael Faraday
explanation: Correct option: (C). Hans Christian Oersted, a professor in Denmark, noticed a compass needle deflect whenever a nearby circuit was closed or opened, showing that electricity and magnetism are linked. Volta and Galvani are associated with electric cells, and Faraday is not the scientist named in this discovery.

stem: A student moves a switch between ON and OFF several times while watching a compass kept under a wire of the circuit. Which set of observations is correct?
options: The needle deflects only when the switch is turned OFF
The needle deflects once and then stays deflected forever
The needle never moves because the wire is not a magnet
The needle deflects when ON and returns when OFF
explanation: Correct option: (D). The magnetic field exists only while current flows, so the needle deflects each time the switch is ON and returns to its original direction each time it is OFF. No current flows when the switch is OFF, so it cannot cause deflection then; the effect does not remain after the current stops; and a wire need not be a magnet to have a magnetic effect while carrying current.

stem: In Activity 4.1, a thin sheet of cardboard is kept between the current-carrying wire and the compass. What will happen when the current is switched ON?
options: The needle still deflects, as the effect acts through it
The needle does not deflect, as cardboard blocks the effect
The needle deflects only if the cardboard is made wet first
The needle deflects only if the wire is touching the compass
explanation: Correct option: (A). A magnetic effect can act through non-magnetic materials kept in between, such as cardboard, so the needle still deflects. Cardboard does not block the field, wetting it is not needed, and the wire does not have to touch the compass because the magnetic field surrounds the wire.

stem: Riya sets up Activity 4.1 but the compass needle does not move at all when she turns the switch ON. Which is the most likely reason?
options: The connecting wire is made of copper and not iron
No current flows, as the cell is dead or a joint is loose
The compass was placed below the wire instead of above it
The switch was made using drawing pins and a safety pin
explanation: Correct option: (B). The needle deflects only when current flows. If the cell is dead or a connection is loose, the circuit is incomplete and there is no magnetic field. Copper wire carries current and produces a magnetic field; the activity itself places the compass beneath the wire; and a drawing-pin switch works when made correctly.

stem: What is an electromagnet?
options: A bar magnet that is wrapped in insulated wire
An iron nail rubbed with a strong magnet
A current-carrying coil that acts as a magnet
A magnet that works only in the Earth's field
explanation: Correct option: (C). A current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet is called an electromagnet. A bar magnet wrapped in wire or a nail rubbed with a magnet does not use current to become a magnet, and an electromagnet's magnetism comes from the current, not from the Earth's field.

stem: Why do most electromagnets used in practical applications have an iron core?
options: The iron core makes the electromagnet stronger
The iron core stops the coil from getting warm
The iron core lets the coil work with no current
The iron core keeps the poles from ever reversing
explanation: Correct option: (A). Inserting an iron nail in the coil made the compass deflect much more and attract clips, so an iron core makes the electromagnet stronger. It does not stop the wire heating, the coil still needs current to be a magnet, and the poles can still be reversed by reversing the current.

stem: The north pole of a compass needle is attracted towards end A of an electromagnet. What are the poles at ends A and B of the coil?
options: End A is north and end B is south
Both ends A and B are north poles
Both ends A and B are south poles
End A is south and end B is north
explanation: Correct option: (D). Unlike poles attract, so the end that attracts the compass's north pole must be a south pole. Like a bar magnet, an electromagnet has two opposite poles, so end B is north. Both ends cannot have the same pole, and calling end A north would mean like poles attract.

stem: Which change will make an electromagnet attract more iron paper clips?
options: Using fewer turns of wire in the coil
Using two cells in place of one cell
Taking the iron nail out of the coil
Reversing the direction of the current
explanation: Correct option: (B). A battery of two cells gives a larger current, which creates a stronger magnetic field, so more clips are attracted. Fewer turns and removing the iron core make the electromagnet weaker, and reversing the current only reverses the poles without changing the strength.

stem: Four coils of the same shape and size are made of iron, copper, aluminium and nichrome wire. Current is passed through each coil with a compass placed nearby. In which coils will the compass needle be deflected?
options: Only in the iron coil
Only in the iron and copper coils
In all four of the coils
Only in the coils that are not nichrome
explanation: Correct option: (C). Any conductor carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field, whatever its material. Iron, copper, aluminium and nichrome all conduct electricity, so all four coils deflect the compass. Believing only iron works confuses a magnetic material with a current-carrying conductor, and nichrome's higher resistance does not stop its magnetic effect.

stem: How does a crane operator make a lifting electromagnet release the iron scrap it is holding?
options: By switching OFF the current in the coil
By reversing the direction of the current
By adding more turns of wire to the coil
By cooling the electromagnet with water

stem: In a scrap yard, iron objects are mixed with aluminium cans. How can a lifting electromagnet help to sort them?
options: It lifts both metals and drops the aluminium first
It lifts the iron only, leaving aluminium behind
It lifts only the aluminium cans, which are lighter
It heats the pile so that the aluminium melts away

It produces the electricity used in our homes
It blocks harmful particles coming from space
It keeps the air warm during the winter season

stem: Sumana forgets to switch OFF her model lifting electromagnet. After some time the nail no longer picks up clips, although the wire around it is still warm. What is the best explanation?
options: The cell has weakened, so the current and the field are too small
The nail has turned into a permanent magnet that repels the clips
The heat in the wire has changed the clips into a non-magnetic metal
The coil has reversed its poles, and reversed poles cannot attract iron
explanation: Correct option: (A). Keeping the circuit connected for a long time weakens the cell, so the current falls and the magnetic field becomes too weak to lift the clips, although a small current can still warm the wire. A magnetised nail would attract, not repel, unmagnetised clips; mild warming does not change iron into a non-magnetic metal; and either pole attracts iron.

stem: Why does a nichrome wire become warm when an electric current flows through it?
options: Its magnetic field rubs against the air around it
Its resistance turns some electrical energy into heat
The cell sends hot liquid from its electrolyte into it
The wire takes in heat from the surroundings
explanation: Correct option: (B). A conductor resists the flow of current, and this resistance converts some electrical energy into heat; this is the heating effect of electric current. A magnetic field does not rub against air, no liquid flows from the cell into the wire, and the wire becomes warmer than its surroundings rather than absorbing heat from them.

stem: The same nichrome wire is connected for 30 s, first to one cell and then to a battery of two cells. Which observation is expected, and why?
options: It heats more with two cells, as the current is larger
It heats more with one cell, as the current is steadier
It heats equally, as the wire and the time are the same
It heats only with one cell, as two cells cancel out
explanation: Correct option: (A). The heat produced depends on the magnitude of the current. Two cells give a larger current, so the wire gets hotter in the same time. One cell gives less current, equal heating ignores the change in current, and cells joined correctly in a battery add up rather than cancel.

stem: Why is nichrome wire, rather than copper wire, used as the heating element in electric heaters?
options: Nichrome is an insulator, so it traps heat inside it
Nichrome is cheaper to make than copper wire is
Nichrome has higher resistance, so it makes more heat
Nichrome is magnetic, so it heats by its magnetic field
explanation: Correct option: (C). Nichrome offers higher resistance than copper of the same size and length, so it generates more heat for a given current. Nichrome is a conductor, not an insulator (otherwise no current would flow); cost is not the reason given; and the heating is due to resistance, not magnetism.

stem: A household socket rated for a small current is used for a high-power room heater, and after some time its plastic parts start melting. What is the best explanation and remedy?
options: The heater's magnetic field melts plastic; keep magnets away
The large current overheats it; use a correctly rated one
The socket is too cold for the heater; warm the socket first
The heater uses too little current; add a second heater nearby
explanation: Correct option: (B). A current larger than the socket is rated for heats its parts strongly (heating effect), which can melt plastic or even cause a fire, so wires, plugs and sockets rated for the current must be used. Magnetism does not melt the plastic, warming the socket makes things worse, and adding another heater increases the current further.

stem: In a Voltaic cell, what is the liquid in which the two metal rods are partly dipped called?
options: Electrode
Carbon paste
Electrolyte
Insulator
explanation: Correct option: (C). The liquid, usually a weak acid or salt solution, is the electrolyte. The metal rods are the electrodes, a carbon paste is not the liquid of a Voltaic cell (a dry cell has a paste-like electrolyte), and an insulator would not allow the cell to work.

stem: How is electricity produced in a Voltaic cell?
options: By a chemical reaction of rods and electrolyte
By heating the electrolyte until it starts to boil
By the magnetic field of the two metal rods
By sunlight falling on the glass container
explanation: Correct option: (A). A chemical reaction between the rods (electrodes) and the electrolyte produces electricity; when the chemicals are used up the cell is dead. Heating, magnetism and sunlight are not how a Voltaic cell works.

stem: Aman connects an LED to his lemon cell, but the LED does not glow. All joints are tight. What should he try first?
options: Replace the copper wires with plastic strips
Reverse the two connections of the LED
Squeeze all the juice out of the lemons
Join the copper wire of each lemon to itself
explanation: Correct option: (B). An LED lets current pass only when its longer lead is joined to the positive terminal and its shorter lead to the negative terminal, so reversing it is the first fix. Plastic strips are not electrodes, removing the juice removes the electrolyte, and joining a wire to itself does not connect the cells in the series needed.

stem: Volta replaced the frog's leg with paper soaked in salt water and still obtained an electric current. What did this show?
options: Electricity can only come from living things
The frog's leg had stored up electricity earlier
Salt water alone can make current without metals
The metals and the liquid produced the current

It disproved Galvani's idea that electricity came from the frog, and the metals were still part of the setup, so salt water alone was not shown to produce current.

stem: Two cells are made with an iron nail and a copper strip: one dipped in lemon juice and the other in pure water. In which case will an LED connected correctly glow, and why?
options: In pure water, because pure water is a good conductor
In both cases, because the same two metals are used
In lemon juice, because it acts as an electrolyte
In neither case, because iron cannot be an electrode
explanation: Correct option: (C). A cell needs an electrolyte, such as lemon juice or a salt solution, for the chemical reaction and to conduct electricity. stem: Reena notices that her two-year-old phone battery needs charging more often than when it was new. Which explanation is correct?

Rechargeable batteries cannot be charged more than once
Her phone battery has changed into a dry cell

stem: Why should used batteries be taken to an e-waste recycling facility rather than thrown in regular garbage?
options: They become fully harmless once they stop working
They can be refilled with lemon juice and used again
They hold harmful and useful materials, such as lead
They give off a strong magnetic field when thrown
explanation: Correct option: (C). A used battery may still contain acids and metals like lead, cadmium, nickel or lithium, which can cause fires or harm the environment, and many of these materials are valuable and can be recycled. A used battery is not completely harmless, it cannot be revived with lemon juice, and it does not produce a strong magnetic field.

stem: Which statement correctly compares a dry cell with a lithium-ion (Li-ion) battery?
options: A dry cell uses a liquid electrolyte, but a Li-ion battery uses none
Both work chemically, but only the Li-ion battery is recharged
A Li-ion battery lasts forever, but a dry cell must be thrown away
A dry cell works by heating, but a Li-ion battery works chemically
explanation: Correct option: (B). Every cell and battery generates current from chemical reactions; a dry cell is single-use, while a Li-ion battery can be recharged and reused. A dry cell has a paste, not a liquid; rechargeable batteries also wear out over time; and a dry cell does not work by heating.
